nodes.title: A checkpoint is not a barrier: the only place a pause can hold is between the worker and the side effect
nodes.body:
SOUNDGATE tested six frameworks against the implied contract of a pause, that while a run is paused, cancelled or timed out no gated side effect executes, and it held on none of them. The dominant mechanism is a sibling leak: the gate suspends its own branch while a sibling branch executes the effect during the pause, so a later rejection cannot prevent it. 215 of 1,200 live runs executed the gated effect while paused.

For us this is not a paper finding, it is a property to check in our own code. Our checkpoints gate a patch promotion, and the worker writes to a worktree that the apply then reads. If a worker in a paused campaign can still write, or if an autopilot tick can start an apply that raced the pause, then a rejection is decorative. The rule to enforce: the apply is the only side effect that crosses the boundary, it reads a frozen patch blob rather than a live directory, and pause takes effect at admission of the next apply rather than on the worker's branch.

The second half is cancellation. Temporal: activities that do not heartbeat cannot receive cancellation, because cancellation is opt-in by the child. A worker that only touches the workspace every few minutes is exactly such a child, so our stop must be enforced by the applier refusing, not by asking the worker to stop.

nodes.title: Two different artifacts: raw traces for diagnosis, itemized claims for injection
nodes.body:
Meta-Harness ablated feedback quality and got 34.6 median accuracy from scores alone, 34.9 from scores plus LLM-written summaries, and 50.0 from raw trace access, with the median full-access candidate beating the best candidate of either ablation. Summaries recovered none of the signal and sometimes hurt. Their proposer read a median 82 files per iteration, about 40 percent prior source and 40 percent execution traces, and navigated by grep rather than ingesting.

That is not an argument against our one-sentence lessons, it is an argument that they answer a different question. A claim is what goes in the next attempt's brief and its job is to be short and actionable; ACE shows the failure mode when a model rewrites the whole accumulated context instead, context collapse took 18,282 tokens to 122 and accuracy from 66.7 to 57.1, below the no-adaptation baseline.

Keep them separate and never let one substitute for the other: itemized claims with helpful and harmful counters plus deterministic pruning for what the worker reads; the immutable ledger and git history for what a policy-level diagnosis reads. We already have both. What we lack is a tool that lets the L2 diagnoser grep the ledger the way Meta-Harness's proposer greps its filesystem. That is a small CLI, not a model.

nodes.title: We cannot allocate what we cannot bill: cost telemetry is a prerequisite, not a nicety
nodes.body:
Our budget is enforced in rounds and minutes because subagent session events carry no token usage, so spentUsd is always zero. Every allocation result surveyed assumes you can count what you spent: SPLIT plans a split across samples, models and verification and lands within 0.8 points of hindsight-optimal while every fixed rule loses at least 2.5 points somewhere; the 42x effort result and the 4x allocation result both need per-task cost.

The measurement side is messier than it looks. In production coding traffic cached input was 97.4 percent of input tokens and 72.9 percent of modelled cost, while on one long well-cached session output was 69 percent of the bill, so no single cost model covers both. Three byte-identical runs cost $0.90, $1.17 and $1.42, a 58 percent spread, and the costlier run failed; the author's rule is to publish rates and shares but never an absolute session cost, and to compare only cost per completed task. Cutting 38.4 percent of tool-output tokens raised the bill 6.8 percent, so a token-count reduction is not a cost win either. There are three registers that must never be blended: billed, estimated, unknown.

Consequence: bill per attempt at the point the usage is emitted, store it with the attempt, and report cost per landed promotion rather than per round. Until then every policy question about model mix, K, or effort escalation is unanswerable and our USD budget is decorative.
nodes.source: arXiv:2610.23255, agentic trace study, context-clock, arXiv:2607.12161

nodes.title: The cheap novel experiment available to us: re-plan candidate count mid-run from the live pass rate
nodes.body:
Adaptive branching is studied only offline: SPLIT, Cohere and the aggregation work all fix the allocation before the run, and the recorded gap is that no published system re-plans K mid-run from a live verifier's observed pass rate. We have exactly the ingredients that gap is missing: a live verifier, a per-task history, and a ledger that already records per-attempt outcomes.

The experiment is small. Pick one task family, compare rounds with K=1 against a rule that raises K only after n consecutive failures on that task and drops back after a pass, and compare cost per landed promotion rather than pass rate. The honest control is the textbook baseline, not the incumbent, because the pre-registered DGM port says a textbook move recovers most of a search loop's gain.

This is worth doing because it is the one place our own loop can produce a number nobody else has, and it is falsifiable with data we already generate. It also forces the verifier-precision and billing work first, since without those the comparison measures noise.

Our verifier is a shell command; its precision is unmeasured.
Zero collected tests exiting 0 is a real instance of low precision looking like success.
minGain is the same acceptor PACE attacks.
Self-Harness held-in and held-out non-regression is the acceptor we should adopt.
Cohere says the lead should implement; we delegate anyway to stay idle.
Silent handoff failures are the mechanism that makes delegation lossy.
The sibling-leak finding is a property our own pause must be checked against.
Traces for diagnosis, claims for injection; do not substitute one for the other.
Compaction summaries are not a substitute for raw trace when diagnosing.
Cached input dominates modelled cost, so a token count is not a bill.
Three registers, never blended: billed, estimated, unknown.
We have the live verifier and per-task history that offline allocation studies lack.
Without verifier precision the K comparison measures noise.
